screens.title: Recap: CRT and the Nervous System
screens.html:
Recap: CRT and the Nervous System

CRT replaces damaged tissues with functional cells. This is vital for the nervous system, where neurons have limited regenerative capacity.

Parkinson's: Replacing dopamine-producing neurons in the Substantia Nigra.

Alzheimer's: Replacing cholinergic neurons or mitigating amyloid plaque damage.

screens.title: Hormones via Recombinant DNA
screens.html:
🔍

Hormones via Recombinant DNA

Before recombinant DNA (rDNA), insulin was harvested from cows and pigs. Today, we use 'biological factories'.

Example

The human gene for insulin is inserted into a bacterial plasmid. The bacteria then translate this human code into functional human insulin proteins.

screens.title: Synthesis of rDNA and Hormones
screens.html:
🧠

Synthesis of rDNA and Hormones

rDNA technology has revolutionised endocrine treatment by providing pure human hormones.

Diabetes Mellitus

Mass-produced insulin via E. coli improves control and prevents allergic reactions.

Growth Disorders

Human Growth Hormone (hGH) is now synthesised to treat pituitary dwarfism.

Remember

Biotech creates structures identical to natural hormones.

screens.title: Impact on Quality of Life
screens.html:
EVALUATION

Impact on Quality of Life

We measure biotech success by Patient Quality of Life (QoL), not just survival.

Reduced frequency of invasive treatments.

Restored independence in neuro-disorder patients.

Prevention of secondary complications like diabetic skin issues.

screens.title: Future Directions: Personalised Medicine
screens.html:
🔑

Future Directions: Personalised Medicine

The 'one size fits all' approach is fading. Pharmacogenomics allows us to tailor drug treatments based on an individual's unique genetic profile.

Key point

Personalised medicine reduces adverse reactions by predicting how a person's metabolic enzymes will process a drug.

screens.title: The Regulatory Pathway: TGA
screens.html:
The Regulatory Pathway: TGA

The TGA regulates all Australian biotech products to ensure safety, quality, and efficacy.

Lab Research - In-vitro and animal testing for safety.

Clinical Trials - Three phases testing human safety and efficacy.

TGA Review - Data assessment for Australian market approval.

screens.title: ETHICS & SOCIETY
screens.html:
ETHICS & SOCIETY

Global Inequities

While we discuss cutting-edge CRT, much of the world lacks access to basic rDNA insulin. This is known as the Biotech Divide.

Health is a human right, but biotechnology is often a luxury. — Anonymous

screens.title: Factors Affecting Access
screens.html:
Factors Affecting Access

Why is life-saving biotech inaccessible?

Cost High R&D drives expensive patents.

Infrastructure Cold-chain storage is often unavailable.

Education Shortage of staff trained for complex therapies.

screens.title: Biotech and Human Evolution
screens.html:
⚠️

Biotech and Human Evolution

Evolution once relied on natural selection. Biotechnology now enables 'directed' evolution.

Biological Evolution

Slow, random mutations; survival of the fittest.

Biotechnological Synthesis

Rapid, intentional changes; editing our genetic code.

Watch out

We are bypassing natural selection's filters.

screens.title: The Genetic Bottleneck?
screens.html:
🤯

The Genetic Bottleneck?

By treating genetic disorders (like Type 1 Diabetes) and allowing individuals to reproduce, we are keeping 'deleterious' alleles in the gene pool.

Fun fact

Biotechnology is effectively stopping certain aspects of natural selection in humans.

screens.title: Evolutionary Impact
screens.html:
Evolutionary Impact

How does biotechnology primarily interfere with the process of natural selection?

1.

By increasing the mutation rate in the atmosphere.

2.

By allowing individuals with previously fatal genetic conditions to survive and pass on their genes.

3.

By making all humans genetically identical through cloning.

4.

By speeding up the process of genetic drift in small populations.

Answers on the next slide...

Personalised vs. Public Health

There is a tension between spending billions on 'boutique' personalised CRT for a few, versus spending that money on public health initiatives for the many.

CRITICAL THINKING

Ethical Considerations of CRT

Reviewing the obstacles to CRT:

Development of teratomas (uncontrolled cell growth).

The 'Moral Status' of embryonic vs. induced pluripotent stem cells.

Informed consent for patients in clinical trials with unknown outcomes.

screens.title: Case Study: Thyroid Dysfunction
screens.html:
🔍

Case Study: Thyroid Dysfunction

Treating hypothyroidism often requires synthetic thyroxine. Biotech ensures a consistent supply that matches human physiology.

Example

Patients on synthetic thyroxine report higher energy levels and better metabolic regulation compared to historical animal-derived extracts.

screens.title: The Genomic Revolution
screens.html:
🔑

The Genomic Revolution

Every tool we have reviewed — from PCR to CRT — relies on our ability to read and rewrite DNA.

Key point

Future doctors will likely view our current medical treatments as 'primitive' compared to the gene-editing precision of the future.

screens.title: Summary: Points of Synthesis
screens.html:
Summary: Points of Synthesis

1

Therapeutic Target

Biotech moves from systemic treatment to cellular replacement (CRT).

2

Genetic Tools

rDNA creates hormonal replacements that are biologically identical to human versions.

3

Global Responsibility

Regulatory bodies (TGA) must balance innovation with safety and equitable access.

screens.title: Final Synthesis Challenge
screens.html:
Final Synthesis Challenge

Assuming cost was not an issue, should we prioritise 'curing' old age and neurodegeneration through CRT, or should we focus on 'editing' the human genome to prevent these diseases from occurring in the first place? Consider the evolutionary and ethical impacts.

screens.title: Final Synthesis Challenge
screens.html:
Final Synthesis Challenge

You might have said...

Prevention via gene editing alters the germline, reducing genetic diversity.

Treatment via CRT improves individual quality of life without genetic change.

Ethically, prevention avoids suffering, while treatment preserves humanity.

✅​

screens.title: Course Reflection
screens.html:
Course Reflection

As you head into your exams, remember that Biotechnology is the intersection of biology, engineering, and ethics. It is about how we use life to save life.

questions.title: Written practice
questions.prompt: Explain why producing neurons from stem cells does not by itself demonstrate an effective treatment for a nervous system disorder.
steps: Cells must have the appropriate specialised properties, survive and function in the affected tissue.
They must integrate appropriately and contribute to the relevant signalling pathways.
Clinical evidence must assess benefits and risks such as rejection, inappropriate growth and adverse effects; laboratory findings alone do not establish effectiveness.

bank.q: Which neurons are a major focus of cell replacement research in Parkinson’s disease?
bank.why: Loss of dopamine-producing neurons is central to the motor features targeted by these approaches.

bank.q: Why must replacement neurons integrate into tissue?
o: Survival alone does not ensure appropriate signalling
bank.why: Functional recovery requires appropriate connections and signalling as well as survival.

bank.q: Why does a promising laboratory result require further evaluation?
o: Safety and clinical effectiveness need evidence in people
bank.why: An experimental mechanism does not by itself establish safe and effective treatment in patients.
